item.title: The Gift of Humor: Relieving Holiday Stress and Spreading Joy
item.description:
Humor

The Gift of Humor: Relieving Holiday Stress and Spreading Joy

Small moments of humor can ease holiday stress and spread lasting joy.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Humor can relieve holiday stress by relaxing the body, lifting emotions, and shifting perspectives.
  • Humor enhances well-being through laughter, mirth, wit, and relational fusion.
  • Small, intentional moments of humor can create joy and strengthen human connections.
  • Sharing humor can inspire others to spread joy, extending its benefits far beyond the original moment.

As the holiday season nears, so does my annual mission to spread a little joy, relieve some stress, and brighten the lives of those around me. Like Johnny Appleseed, who scattered seeds wherever he traveled, I roam the world planting moments of joy. My seeds, however, are not apples. What are they? I'll keep you guessing for a moment. But here's a hint: They're sprinkled with humor.

Every December, I wear a round pin approximately two inches in diameter. It features a green letter “L” surrounded by a red circle with a diagonal slash through it—much like a no-smoking sign.

When people ask what it means, I invite them to figure it out. After all, much of the pleasure of humor comes from “getting it.”

Need a hint? Think Christmas. The red slash means “No,” so the pin says “No L.” Say it aloud. Got it? No-L. Noel!

When people solve the puzzle, their faces often light up. They smile, chuckle, or express delight. For a moment, their attention shifts from whatever occupied their minds to the pleasure of discovering something amusing. Often, that brief moment of delight becomes a pleasant memory that continues to bring a smile long after the encounter.

I don’t know what stresses or worries someone may be carrying when we meet, but I do know that, for a brief moment, we can share an experience of discovery, delight, and human connection. You don’t have to know someone’s struggles to offer them a moment of joy, and, at times of holiday stress, that moment of joy is often exactly what someone needs.

How does my little No-L pin connect with holiday stress, anxiety, and depression? In more ways than you might imagine. Although the holidays are often associated with joy and celebration, they can also bring financial pressures, family tensions, loneliness, and grief. For some people, these experiences contribute to increased stress, anxiety, or depressed mood. Humor offers one way to soften these experiences and create moments of emotional relief.

Humor offers four interconnected pathways for relieving distress and enhancing well-being—not only during the holidays but throughout the year (Sultanoff, 2026). First, humor may activate laughter, which can produce pleasurable physical sensations, relieve muscle tension, and promote relaxation. Research also suggests that laughter may reduce cortisol, a hormone involved in the body’s stress response.

Second, humor can activate mirth, the emotional experience of joy, uplift, and pleasure associated with humor—even when laughter is absent. Mirth can soften emotional distress and introduce pleasurable feelings.

Third, humor engages wit, a cognitive response. Wit involves recognizing incongruities, discovering unexpected meanings, and shifting perspectives. Because our interpretations influence our emotional experiences, wit can help us see difficult situations differently.

When someone “gets” my No-L pin, they experience wit through the discovery of an unexpected meaning. That moment of recognition can temporarily shift attention away from worries or distress.

Shakespeare captured the relationship between thinking and feeling in Hamlet: “There is nothing either good or bad, but thinking makes it so.” Shakespeare reminds us that how we interpret events influences how we experience them. Our circumstances matter, but so does the meaning we assign to them. Humor can introduce alternative perspectives, interrupt negative thinking patterns, and encourage greater cognitive flexibility. These shifts may lead to a reduction in emotional distress and enable us to respond more effectively to life’s challenges.

Finally, humor can activate Relational Fusion, the interpersonal connection that develops through shared humorous experiences. Humor can serve as both social glue, strengthening relationships, and social lubricant, easing interpersonal tension.

Even a brief humorous encounter between strangers can create a moment of connection. These experiences may help buffer stress, reduce feelings of isolation, and enhance well-being.

My No-L pin creates more than a moment of delight. Whenever someone solves its mystery (with a little prompting, that is practically everyone), I give them a pin of their own. The real gift is not the pin itself, but the experience it creates—and the opportunity for that experience to be shared again.

What begins as a playful puzzle becomes a shared experience, a gift, and sometimes a connection that lasts for years. For decades, I have been scattering No-L pins throughout the world. During the holidays, I occasionally encounter restaurant servers, store clerks, and others still wearing pins I gave them years earlier.

Without realizing it, I have recruited an army of Santa’s little helpers who continue spreading humor and delight. These encounters remind me that a small humorous interaction can have effects that extend well beyond the original moment. My little seeds of playfulness have taken root!

We can all intentionally create small moments of humor that enrich our lives and those of the people around us. My No-L pin is only one of my holiday traditions. I also wear playful holiday hats and sweatshirts designed to invite smiles and spark conversations.

As a longtime Star Trek fan, one of my favorite Christmas sweatshirts features a decorated tree with the caption, “Trek the Halls.” Perhaps you have a favorite piece of holiday clothing or other holiday props that could tickle someone’s funny bone.

During my years as a professional speaker, I gave away thousands of red clown noses. Fortunately, I still have a stockpile, and with a little holiday magic, those clown noses have transformed into Rudolph noses! I wear one myself and give them to others who want to spread a little holiday cheer.

You don’t need a No-L pin, a Rudolph nose, or a Star Trek Christmas sweatshirt to spread holiday humor. A playful observation, an unexpected twist, or a moment of shared amusement can brighten someone’s day.

Humor won’t eliminate life’s stresses, but it can change how we experience them. It can relax the body, lift our spirits, refresh our thinking, and strengthen our connections with others.

This holiday season, consider becoming a Johnny Appleseed of humor. Plant a little joy wherever you go. You never know how far those seeds may travel—or how long they may continue to grow.

item.title: Exploring the Psyche During a Psychedelic Session
item.description:
Psychedelics

Exploring the Psyche During a Psychedelic Session

How I approach the exploratory phase of psychedelic psychotherapy.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • There are many stages during psychedelic psychotherapy; the exploratory phase is one of them.
  • Psychedelic psychotherapists can use the material that arises in session to move toward therapeutic goals.
  • The therapist helps connect emerging experiences to goals while staying open to unexpected insights.

I believe that discovering, speaking, and living our truths, along with unconditional self-love, are the true medicines for our wounded hearts and traumatized bodies. Psychedelic psychotherapy (PAT) helps us access both.

Each session of PAT is different, and like any kind of therapy, the actual process and results depend on each individual person. I use a 5-phase framework for my sessions, which helps me better work with where the client is. The phases include: grounding and dropping in; on-set of the medicine; therapeutic exploration; coming down; wrapping up. I will focus on the exploratory phase in this post.

In the exploratory phase, we examine everything that comes up and arises in the client's consciousness: images, sounds, shapes, textures, sensations, stories, memories, and emotions. This might include: doors, fields, stars, space, pyramids, forests, tunnels, catacombs, coffins, insects, trees, father, mother, sister, aunt, basements, and creatures known and new. Not everything has meaning, but we must explore and discover what does. The client is the explorer of the cosmos and their own psyche. The therapist is a guide, a psychological surgeon, a trusted friend, a confidant, and an attendant in this process. Good exploratory questions are essential here. These don’t always have to be therapeutic, but they do help the client deepen their relationship with what is surfacing in the present moment. I might ask:

Where does that door lead?

Where is the train going?

What is it like being a marshmallow?

What does that memory mean to you?

Why is that coming up now for you?

Where do you feel that in your body?

Sometimes the meaning is obvious. Personal memories surface and demand to be acknowledged. One man in his thirties came for our ketamine protocol to deal with how his PTSD symptoms were affecting his relationship. He was scared in almost every situation, always worried the worst was going to happen. During the first session, he was hesitant to talk about his parents, simply saying they were good to him and he didn’t want to speak badly of them. To me, this is always a sure sign the truth is being partially spoken but mostly hidden. My job is to encourage a deeper exploration of feelings about our younger years, the time when we were most obviously programmed by our caregivers. He said his mom worried all the time, and he didn’t want to worry his mom more by stating his needs or by doing things his way. During his second session, he started to recall what it was like living with his father, who was a Marine. When he was around ten years old, his father would make him spar and wrestle — essentially do tactical drills — to protect himself and to avoid being “taken by surprise,” or, worse, “hostage.” This was not martial arts training but rather punishing preparation in case the worst happened. Dad said it was bound to. So be prepared.

Think about that — being ten and being physically forced by your father to prepare yourself to fend off people trying to abduct you. How would that affect your sense of self, safety, and trust in others? He started to see how, from a very young age, he was being programmed by his father, and his mother, who allowed this training to happen, to see the world as dangerous, to always be prepared for the scariest and worst kinds of danger. (Even later, when he cognitively realized he would most likely not ever be in such scary circumstances, his body and brain continued to reinforce those original messages, keeping him on constant alert.)

After three sessions, he was able to hold love for his parents but also speak to his anger and his utter dismay at being raised that way. He began to regulate his own nervous system and change the initial programming so that he could see the world as it is, not as his father had trained him to see it.

Sometimes in session, feelings and images seem random but turn out to be significant. A woman in her thirties suffered over half her life with agoraphobia and panic attacks. She could barely be around people for fear of being embarrassed about something she might do “that was dumb or stupid.” This fear kept her from socializing and from engaging in activities outside her home, and she struggled just to leave her house. During one ketamine session, she said she was being smothered by a marshmallow. She struggled to breathe and felt panic coming on. I guessed that this was what it must have felt like to live with agoraphobia and that intense fear of being scrutinized and judged. She immediately understood this to be true for herself. I asked if she could find the edges and look beyond the marshmallow. She said there was vast space, with stars. I asked how it felt. She said freeing and calming. I asked where the marshmallow was, and she said it had shrunk down to a small spot in her awareness. I encouraged her to continue changing the scope of her awareness, from the suffocating feeling to the greater sense of spaciousness.

Days later, she reported that while standing at her refrigerator, she felt the usual feeling of panic arising, but then she opened her awareness to the whole kitchen around her. She immediately calmed herself and realized she was safe. After three ketamine therapy sessions, she went to a concert, then to a friend’s party, and signed up for a 5k race. These three activities are a huge success for someone who could barely leave her home without panicking. She continues to struggle with anxiety but now knows how to care for herself while moving toward what helps her thrive.

The psychedelic psychotherapy experience can be many things—exciting, frightening, confusing, frustrating, complex, simple, full, and empty. One role of the client is to be an explorer, to be simply curious, open, and trusting, and to surrender during the process. One role of the therapist is to help the client make sense of the experience and the material that arises during the journey in relation to the client’s transformational goals and intentions. However, the medicine does what the medicine will, so we must remain open to where the medicine and the client’s wisdom and intuitive senses take us.

item.title: How Emotional Contagion Can Impact a Workplace
item.description:
Emotional Contagion

How Emotional Contagion Can Impact a Workplace

Moods of all kinds travel quickly among an employee population.

Posted October 13, 2026

I was recently speaking with someone who runs a successful 40-person business. Until just a couple weeks ago, it had been a highly productive, generally problem-free environment.

Emotions can unconsciously pass easily from one person to another.
Source: Alexander Suhorucov / Pexels

Then one day in a meeting an employee made a negative comment about a relatively minor aspect of the company's benefit program that had never before been a problem. (I've changed a few details here to protect the company's privacy.) Not long after the meeting, the manager returned to his office and found that another employee just wrote him a frustrated email about the same issue. A few minutes later, yet another upset employee stopped by his office and wanted to call a staff meeting about it.

The business owner was both puzzled and disturbed. What was going on? Suddenly a business that was humming nicely along the track seemed to have been taken off the rails by a problem that, until earlier that morning, hadn't been a problem at all.

Fertile Breeding Ground

Moods of course are fluid, not static, and change readily. Furthermore, they do not exist in isolation; in a workplace environment, networks of teams, alliances, friendships, and antagonisms provide a fertile breeding ground for all kinds of emotions to circulate throughout an employee population.

Emotional contagion occurs when people, often unconsciously, mimic or pick up the feelings of others they are interacting with.

Everyone understandably has opinions and feelings about work, and those feelings (both positive and negative) are frequently shared with others. Yet the concept of "emotional contagion" is seldom discussed, or even recognized, in the business world. In nearly a quarter century of management, plus an MBA program, I never once heard the phrase mentioned.

Both Negative and Positive

Personally, I tend to think of emotional contagion in the workplace as a kind of accelerant. It amplifies feelings. It can be a positive, motivating force, as well as a negative one.

When people spend a great deal of time working together in close proximity, in a setting as important to an individual's financial and emotional well-being as work, there are usually plenty of feelings to be shared.

In the circumstance described at the outset, the sharing of feelings caused difficulties for management, since what started as one person's gripe quickly turned into a broader organizational problem. The whole became larger than the sum of its parts.

However, as a longtime employee and manager myself, I've also seen the upside to this phenomenon. I've been part of situations where employee enthusiasm for things like, say, a new, creative company advertising campaign or a generous new employee bonus program gathered momentum of its own and generated genuine, widespread positive excitement.

Bottom line: Emotional contagion is a subtle, but recognized force that both managers and employees can benefit from being aware of as they navigate the often challenging emotional landscape of the workplace.

item.title: 7 Strategies to Get Others to See Things Your Way
item.description:
Persuasion

7 Strategies to Get Others to See Things Your Way

These insights can help you get people to change their minds.

Posted October 13, 2026

Who is persuading whom?
Source: Mircea Iancu / Pixabay

Thumbing through my many years of blog posts on this site, I found that the two times I wrote about changing someone’s mind rate among my most popular posts. It appears that a lot of us are frustrated over how hard it is to convince others—family members, friends, or strangers whose opinions we know via social or other media—that our own views are the better ones.

A dear cousin of mine can no longer discuss newsworthy topics with her sister, as each of them inevitably gives up, saying to the other, “I don’t know how you can feel that way!” If only they were willing and able to explore which experiences led them to take up such divergent views.

I’ve discovered some fresh insights about this quandary in books by experts in a variety of fields. Whether your goal is mainly to engage more pleasantly with family over Thanksgiving, or to become better at influencing others in the wider world, here are some promising suggestions.

  1. Start small. If you’re timid or not yet certain how to approach someone who thinks differently without coming across as too confrontational, choose a modest goal. More people may refuse to engage with you in a conversation about opinions than will participate fully with you, notes David McRaney, author of How Minds Change: The New Science of Belief, Opinion, and Persuasion. That applies to relatives, too, so learn when to move on.
  2. Be aware of tribal thinking. McRaney, in his chapter “The Truth is Tribal,” writes that maintaining a person’s group identity is extremely important to them, and if you’re going to make headway in changing someone’s mind, you must understand the strength of that drive to protect themselves.
  3. Assume good will, whether struggling with marital disagreements or during conversations with someone outside your usual circle. Unless you strongly suspect that your conversational opposite is a mean, unfeeling, and selfish person, be empathetic first and ask for explanations for their beliefs, rather than announcing yours.
  4. Find doors that are already half-open and push gently on them, suggests Daniel Fried, author of The Activist: A Daoist Protest Manual. Along those lines, a study by political scientist David Redlawsk and his colleagues, discussed in depth by McRaney, found that there is “a quantifiable level of doubt when we admit we are likely wrong and become compelled to update our beliefs, attitudes, and values.” And if that level isn’t reached, you (the would-be opinion-shifter) can try to convince someone of the incongruities of their stand, but it only makes them feel more certain.
  5. Broaden your thoughts about “change.” That includes paying attention to what has been learned about what actually works to get people to change their minds. For example, see McRaney’s chapter on “street epistemology,” in which he explains how to establish rapport and how to clarify and use your interlocutor’s definitions for his claims.
  6. Increase your power and influence by joining like-minded others. Roy Speckhardt, author of Creating Change Through Humanism, suggests getting involved in local chapters of national groups whose values you share.
  7. Take stock of your skills. If knocking on doors or speaking directly to those in authority makes you too nervous, use whatever abilities you have to persuade. Writing letters or a story, or creating art of any kind, can cause ripples in the real world, as does pondering how you and those who trust your opinions spend, invest, or donate your money. You don’t have to be a so-called influencer to influence others.
